anchorData:
ALL FIGURES ARE ILLUSTRATIVE (made-up). Currency is Kenya Shillings (KES). 

STALL STOCK (bought in bulk) and MARKED PRICES:
| Item | Qty | Cost price each | Total cost | Marked price each | Expected sales at marked price |
| Maize flour (2 kg bag) | 20 | 120 | 2,400 | 150 | 3,000 |
| Mandazi packs | 50 | 40 | 2,000 | 60 | 3,000 |
| Club T-shirts | 40 | 250 | 10,000 | 350 | 14,000 |
| TOTAL | | | 14,400 | | 20,000 |

ORIGINAL (PLANNED) BUDGET, drawn in Lesson 1: Income: expected sales 20,000. Expenditure: stock 14,400 + stall costs (posters, table hire) 600 = 15,000. Planned surplus = 20,000 - 15,000 = 5,000. The plan forgot discounts and commission.

OPEN DAY (ACTUAL): The club put up a '10% OFF' sign. Every item sold. 
| Item | Marked price | Discount each | Selling price | Qty sold | Actual sales | Discount given in total |
| Maize flour | 150 | 15 | 135 | 20 | 2,700 | 300 |
| Mandazi pack | 60 | 6 | 54 | 50 | 2,700 | 300 |
| T-shirt | 350 | 35 | 315 | 40 | 12,600 | 1,400 |
| TOTAL | | | | | 18,000 | 2,000 |
Discount is 10% of the marked price on each item (15/150, 6/60, 35/350). Total discount = 300 + 300 + 1,400 = 2,000, so actual sales = 20,000 - 2,000 = 18,000.

COMMISSION: Halima Mohamed sold the T-shirts and earns 5% commission on T-shirt sales: 5% of 12,600 = 630 (630 / 12,600 x 100 = 5%). Commission is paid out of the cash box.

CASH BOX: Cash box at day's end = 18,000 - 630 = 17,370. Budget expected 20,000. Shortfall = 20,000 - 17,370 = 2,630 = discounts 2,000 + commission 630. (The 600 stall costs and the 14,400 stock were paid earlier from club funds, not from the cash box.)

ACTUAL BUDGET (Lesson 2): Actual income 18,000. Actual expenditure = 14,400 + 600 + 630 = 15,630. Actual surplus = 18,000 - 15,630 = 2,370 (planned was 5,000, so 2,630 less; same gap as the cash box).

PROFIT AND LOSS (Lesson 5), profit = selling price - cost price, percentage on COST price:
| Item | Total cost | Actual sales | Profit | % profit |
| Maize flour | 2,400 | 2,700 | 300 | 12.5% |
| Mandazi | 2,000 | 2,700 | 700 | 35% |
| T-shirts | 10,000 | 12,600 | 2,600 | 26% |
| All goods | 14,400 | 18,000 | 3,600 | 25% |
At marked prices the profit would have been 20,000 - 14,400 = 5,600. After commission and stall costs the club's net gain is 3,600 - 630 - 600 = 2,370 (equals actual surplus). Loss example (illustrative extension): 5 mandazi packs went stale and sold at 30 each (cost 40): loss 10 per pack, 50 in total, percentage loss = 10/40 x 100 = 25%.

OTHER COMMISSION PRACTICE (illustrative, not part of the stall): a Kisumu salesperson earns 8% on sales of 25,000 = 2,000.

MOMBASA TRIP: A Mombasa marine-park guide quotes an education-talk fee of USD 30. At the selling rate this costs 30 x 129.50 = KES 3,885. The trip's only funding is the actual surplus of 2,370, so there is a deficit of 3,885 - 2,370 = 1,515. The planned surplus of 5,000 would have covered it with 1,115 to spare.

EXCHANGE RATE TABLE (Nyali Forex Bureau, Mombasa; illustrative), KES per 1 unit of foreign currency:
| Currency | Bureau BUYS (pays you KES) | Bureau SELLS (you pay KES) |
| 1 US dollar (USD) | 128.00 | 129.50 |
| 1 Euro (EUR) | 139.00 | 141.00 |
| 1 British pound (GBP) | 163.00 | 165.50 |
Lesson 6 (KES to foreign, use SELLING rate, divide): USD 30 costs KES 3,885; KES 7,050 buys EUR 50 (7,050/141); KES 8,275 buys GBP 50 (8,275/165.5); KES 5,000 buys USD 38.61 (5,000/129.50, to 2 d.p.). 
Lesson 7 (foreign to KES, use BUYING rate, multiply): USD 50 gives KES 6,400; EUR 50 gives KES 6,950; GBP 20 gives KES 3,260. 
Tourist round trip: Mr Daniel Brooks changes USD 100 at the buying rate: 100 x 128 = KES 12,800. He changes all KES 12,800 back at the selling rate: 12,800/129.50 = USD 98.84 (2 d.p.). He gets USD 1.16 less (about KES 150). The gap between the rates is KES 1.50 per USD, about 1.2% of the selling rate; this is the bureau's margin.
characters: Mazingira Club: environment club of Lake View Secondary School, Kisumu (fictional school), 40 T-shirts, 20 bags of maize flour and 50 mandazi packs for the open-day stall; goal is to fund a Mombasa trip. Achieng Otieno: club chairperson, leads the brainstorm on raising funds and draws the first budget. Wafula Barasa: club treasurer, keeps the cash box and counts KES 17,370. Halima Mohamed: member who sells T-shirts and earns 5% commission (KES 630). Mr Kiprono Langat: teacher patron, asks 'where did the money go?'. Mr Daniel Brooks: tourist who changes USD 100 at Nyali Forex Bureau, Mombasa (fictional bureau) and gets USD 98.84 back. Mombasa marine-park guide: quotes the USD 30 talk fee. The open day: all goods sold at 10% off. Ugali, sukuma wiki and githeri may be used only as background context; no extra stall figures may be invented beyond the fact sheet.
outcome: The cash box held KES 17,370, not the budgeted 20,000, because the budget assumed every item would sell at the marked price and ignored two costs: 10% discounts (KES 2,000 less income) and Halima's 5% commission on T-shirts (KES 630 paid out), a total gap of KES 2,630. Every item did sell and the club still made a profit of KES 3,600 on stock costing KES 14,400 (25%), but after commission and stall costs the net surplus was only KES 2,370, which is KES 1,515 short of the KES 3,885 guide fee. The tourist's money did not vanish either: the bureau buys dollars at a lower rate (128.00) than it sells them (129.50), so changing KES back gives fewer dollars (USD 98.84 from USD 100). A good plan puts discounts, commission and exchange margins into the budget before the event, and prices items so that the club gains rather than loses.
conventions: All figures are illustrative; label them so. Money is written KES 17,370 or 17,370 with commas; foreign amounts USD 98.84 to 2 d.p. Budget: income = money expected in, expenditure = money expected out; surplus = income - expenditure (positive), deficit = expenditure - income (income smaller), balanced = equal. Marked price = price before discount; discount = marked price - selling price; % discount = discount / marked price x 100. Commission = percentage of sales value earned by the salesperson; % commission = commission / sales x 100. Profit = selling price - cost price; loss = cost price - selling price; % profit or % loss = profit or loss / cost price x 100 (always on cost price). Exchange rates are KES per 1 unit of foreign currency; 'buying rate' and 'selling rate' are from the BUREAU's point of view: bureau buys foreign currency (pays fewer KES) and sells it (charges more KES). KES to foreign: divide by the selling rate. Foreign to KES: multiply by the buying rate. Conversions ignore bureau fees and commission; this is a simplification. Percentages are given exactly as in anchorData; use the term 'actual sales' for 18,000 and 'cash box' only for 17,370. Teaching terms: use 'planned' vs 'actual'. Competency/values/PCI wording must be copied verbatim from the KICD text: Citizenship, Critical thinking and problem solving, Peace, Patriotism, Financial literacy. Key inquiry questions: 1. Why do we need a budget? 2. Why are discounts and commissions necessary?

lessonMap.focus: The puzzling cash box and a first budget
lessonMap.teaches: How to draw a simple budget with income lines and expenditure lines for a club project, after brainstorming ways to raise funds (outcome a)
lessonMap.buildsOn: Nothing earlier; launches the phenomenon (cash box 17,370 versus 20,000 expected).
lessonMap.usesData: Stall stock and marked prices table, planned budget (income 20,000, expenditure 15,000, planned surplus 5,000), and the cash box 17,370 shown as the puzzle.

lessonMap.focus: Planned versus actual: balancing and revising the budget
lessonMap.teaches: How to compare planned and actual figures, classify a budget as surplus, deficit or balanced, and revise it, so that learners see why a budget is needed (outcome a)
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 1: the planned budget with income and expenditure lines.
lessonMap.usesData: Planned budget versus actual budget (income 18,000, expenditure 15,630, surplus 2,370), trip deficit of 1,515 against guide fee 3,885; discount and commission named but not yet calculated.

lessonMap.teaches: How to calculate discount, selling price and percentage discount from marked price (outcome b)
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 2: the actual income was 2,630 below plan, and the gap involved the '10% OFF' sign.
lessonMap.usesData: Open day table: marked price, discount each, selling price, total discount 2,000 for maize flour, mandazi, T-shirts.

lessonMap.teaches: How to calculate commission and percentage commission on sales, and who earns commission (outcome c)
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 3: T-shirt actual sales of 12,600 after the discount.
lessonMap.usesData: Halima's commission 630 on T-shirt sales 12,600 (5%), the 8% salesperson practice example (2,000 on 25,000), and the cash box 17,370 = 18,000 - 630.

lessonMap.focus: Profit and loss on the stall goods
lessonMap.teaches: How to find profit or loss and percentage profit or loss on cost price (outcome d)
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 3 (selling prices) and Lesson 4 (commission as a cost); Lesson 1 cost prices.
lessonMap.usesData: Profit and loss table (cost 14,400, sales 18,000, profit 3,600, 25%), net gain after commission and stall costs 2,370, stale mandazi loss example (25%).

lessonMap.focus: Changing Kenya Shillings into foreign currency for the Mombasa trip
lessonMap.teaches: How to read an exchange rate table and convert KES to foreign currency using the bureau's selling rate (outcome e)
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 2: trip funding deficit; Lesson 5 only for the idea of a margin between buying and selling.

lessonMap.focus: Changing foreign currency back and why the money shrinks
lessonMap.teaches: How to convert foreign currency to KES using the buying rate, and explain why the buying rate is lower than the selling rate so a round trip returns less (outcome e)
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 6: the exchange rate table and conversion from KES.
lessonMap.usesData: Buying-rate conversions (USD 50 = 6,400; EUR 50 = 6,950; GBP 20 = 3,260) and Mr Brooks's round trip: USD 100 to KES 12,800 to USD 98.84, loss USD 1.16, margin KES 1.50 per USD.

lessonMap.focus: Final money model: solving the cash box puzzle
lessonMap.teaches: How to combine budget, discount, commission, profit and exchange in one money model, explain the cash box and shrinking-dollar puzzle, and present everyday uses of commercial arithmetic (outcome f)
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 1-7: planned budget, discount, commission, profit, and the buying/selling gap.
lessonMap.usesData: All anchor data: 20,000 planned, 2,000 discount, 630 commission, 17,370 cash box, 2,630 gap, profit 3,600 (25%), surplus 2,370, trip deficit 1,515, Mr Brooks's USD 98.84.
